question.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}+y={u}_{\pi }(t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\pi )\,,\,y(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi }(t)=u(t-\pi )$ is the unit step function.

You may make use of the following result:

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0
$$

$Y(s)=$
{{field-1}},$\,s>0$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}+y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi }(t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\pi )\} \\ L\{{y}^{′}\}+L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi }(t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\pi )\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{′}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0:$

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
{u}_{\pi }(t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\pi )
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=\pi $ and $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\pi ).$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed sinusoidal forcing. 

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-\pi )\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\pi )\} & ={e}^{-\pi s}\cdot L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡((t+\pi )-\pi )\} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi s}\cdot L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi s}\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi s}}{{s}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}\}+L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi }(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\pi )\} \\ sY(s)+Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi s}}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi s}}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi s}}{({s}^{2}+1)(s+1)}\end{aligned}
$$
